articles.title: Democrats in Washington Move to Ban Data Centers on Public Lands

paras.t: A dozen Democrats in Congress are calling for limiting or banning the construction of data centers on public lands. The moves follow reporting from ProPublica that revealed Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, who leads the White House’s artificial intelligence push, has tens of millions of dollars invested in AI companies.

“Our public lands aren’t a piggy bank for Trump’s powerful friends,” Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto of Nevada said in a social media post that pointed to ProPublica’s reporting. Her office told the news organization that the senator, who serves on the Energy and Natural Resources Committee, is working on legislation to regulate data centers on public lands and will use the panel’s oversight authority to address concerns about transparency surrounding them.

Burgum was asked about ProPublica’s reporting at a recent event hosted by the conservative website Daily Caller. He said that his financial reporting and ethics were “clean as a whistle,” and that he invested in software companies before they turned to AI. “I don’t even know all the names of the companies that are in the portfolio,” he said of his vast wealth.

ProPublica found that hundreds of President Donald Trump’s political appointees in the executive branch, or their spouses, held stocks, owned equity or had other financial ties to AI companies and data center developers. Other offices, including the Environmental Protection Agency and the U.S. Department of Agriculture, defended their political leadership, saying the appointees followed lawyers’ guidance and had not violated ethics rules.

Our reporting also found that a U.S. Geological Survey study released earlier this year identified an area of U.S. Department of the Interior land nearly the size of Montana that might be suitable for data centers.
Several members of Congress pledged to float legislation to ban data center development on this land.

“These lands are treasured and must be protected for future generations to benefit from and enjoy,” Rep. Maxine Dexter of Oregon said in a statement. In mid-November, she filed the Protecting Our Public Lands from Data Centers Act, which would ban data center construction on land managed by the Interior Department and the Forest Service.

Rep. Rashida Tlaib of Michigan in July filed the No AI Data Centers on Federal Lands Act, which would also prohibit their build-out on federally managed land. The measure was dead on arrival in the Republican-controlled House of Representatives.

“I’m going to continue building the coalition for our bill, and at the same time, I’m going to push the Oversight Committee to investigate the outrageous corruption of the Trump Administration,” she told ProPublica in a statement.
The White House did not respond to a request for comment on the pushback from Democrats in Congress.

Also speaking up were Rep. Jared Huffman of California and Sen. Martin Heinrich of New Mexico, who serve as the ranking members of the natural resources committees in their respective chambers. Huffman and Heinrich are in line to take up the gavel in those committees in January when Democrats retake the majority.
“These lands belong to the American people, not private interests looking to cash in,” Heinrich said in a statement. “Public lands belong in public hands.”

Heinrich is pushing the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, a generational overhaul of the legislation governing how federal agencies permit major developments. Republicans in Congress and the White House support the swift passage of the bill, as do some Democrats. The more environmentally minded members of the Democratic caucus, however, are calling on Heinrich to slow down and force a better deal once Congress reconvenes next year with Democratic majorities.

Environmental policy experts agree that permitting reform is desperately needed to address climate change by allowing the faster build-out of renewable electricity generation and transmission lines. But green groups including the Sierra Club, Natural Resources Defense Council and League of Conservation Voters oppose the bill because it would likely also lead to more fossil fuel projects while limiting input on projects from Native American tribes.

The legislation presents a mixed bag for data centers. A spokesperson for Heinrich defended the permitting reform bill, pointing out that it would require data center companies to bear their own costs for connecting to and upgrading the electrical grid. But the legislation would also streamline approval of natural gas-fired power plants, which power many data centers. The bill would make it more difficult to take away a permit after it’s issued.

Meanwhile, the Interior Department released a five-year strategic plan last week that includes a proposal to sell off public lands or pursue “strategic rights-of-way agreements, land exchanges and direct transfer of lands.” It is unclear whether the department intends to offer to sell to companies or only to local, state and tribal governments. Researchers who study natural resources policy told ProPublica that the country’s foundational land management law lays out steps that must be followed to dispose of federal land, steps that will be difficult for the Trump administration to legally navigate.

Still, with permits for data centers pending before the Interior Department, the release of the strategic plan sparked fear that developers might try to buy federal land. Jayson O’Neill, spokesperson for conservation group Save Our Parks, said the plan was another attempt by Burgum to “sell off what’s left to AI data center developers and his extractive resource buddies.”
The Interior Department did not respond to a request for comment on its proposal to sell federal land.

articles.title: Ethics Watchdog Urges Investigation Into Top Health Official, Alleging Conflict of Interest Over Hormone Therapy Policy

paras.t: A nonpartisan ethics watchdog group has asked for an investigation into whether a top Department of Health and Human Services official violated ethics laws after a recent ProPublica investigation revealed actions experts called “alarming” and an “obvious conflict of interest.”

Alicia Jackson, who heads the Advanced Research Projects Agency for Health, publicly endorsed a change to federal health policy on hormone replacement therapies while owning stock in a company that provides access to menopause treatments.

In a letter to the department’s inspector general, the Campaign Legal Center also questioned whether Jackson properly identified up to $400 million in underlying assets held by her husband’s investment firm. The center’s review identified an additional potential conflict — investments in a second firm that provides hormone treatments for menopause.
Jackson, who heads the HHS agency that invests taxpayer money in medical technology and research, was recently placed on administrative leave, though health officials have not publicly explained why.

In its letter, the Campaign Legal Center cited the ProPublica investigation that found Jackson spoke at an HHS press conference last November and was quoted in a department news release announcing the decision to remove “black box warnings” from hormone replacement therapy products.

At the time, Jackson owned at least $115,000 in stock and an unknown amount of stock options in Evernow, a company she founded that connects women to hormone replacement treatments, according to her financial disclosures.

It’s unclear what role, if any, Jackson played in the decision to drop the requirement to display a black box warning, the most serious type of federal safety warning. The Food and Drug Administration regulates drugs. And an FDA panel of experts had recommended ending the requirement months before Jackson became her agency’s director in October 2025.

Still, ethics experts noted that federal law prohibits government employees from participating “personally and substantially” in matters that could influence their personal finances — even making statements at a press conference or in a news release.

The Campaign Legal Center asked the inspector general to examine whether Jackson broke federal ethics laws by failing to recuse herself. Neither Jackson nor the HHS will say whether she obtained a conflict-of-interest waiver before participating in the policy announcement.
“Americans have a right to know that government decisions are not being made to benefit a federal employee’s financial interests,” the organization wrote.
The center also asked the inspector general to determine if Jackson failed to fully and accurately disclose her and her spouse’s financial interests in private investment funds.

ProPublica’s investigation found that Jackson reported she and her husband owned more than 60 venture capital and private equity funds that she said do not disclose their holdings to investors. These include at least 13 funds managed by 137 Ventures, a venture capital firm co-founded by her husband, Alex Jacobson. The company invests in a wide range of industries, including healthcare, digital health and medical device companies.
Ethics experts said the funds could pose a serious conflict of interest if the underlying businesses received grants or contracts from her agency.

The Campaign Legal Center’s review of Jackson’s disclosures identified one of those funds — 137 Ventures IV LP — as an investor in Thirty Madison Inc., a virtual healthcare company. Thirty Madison owns a subsidiary that provides hormone replacement treatments for women experiencing menopause symptoms. Jackson’s disclosures do not show her divesting from the fund before the black box warning announcement, the center said.

Under federal law, financial disclosure forms filed by federal officials like Jackson must then be certified by ethics staff as complying with the law. But Jackson’s two financial disclosures — filed last October and two months ago — remain uncertified.

HHS’ inspector general’s office would not confirm or deny whether it is investigating Jackson. The inspector general, T. March Bell, was one of nearly 100 appointees confirmed by the Senate in a December 2025 party-line vote. President Donald Trump fired the previous inspector general just days into the president’s second term.

ProPublica also requested responses from HHS, Jackson, Jacobson and 137 Ventures, but none commented. In a statement to ProPublica last month, an HHS spokesperson said that while Jackson was on leave the agency would “assess the facts before determining any change in her status. HHS requires all officials to comply with federal ethics laws, regulations, and policies.”

Jackson was appointed by Trump as her agency’s second director and sworn in on Oct. 20, 2025. The agency, created three years earlier to spur revolutionary biomedical research and technologies, has a $1.5 billion budget. It has issued numerous contracts and grants, including $160 million for genetic medicines combating rare diseases and $144 million to study existing treatments for age-related illnesses.

Jackson’s disclosures are among 2,400 added last month to ProPublica’s Trump Team Financials database, a searchable tool launched in March. The records detail the finances of more than 2,300 officials appointed by Trump. Since last year, we’ve requested disclosure records from 127 federal agencies and the White House. Disclosures from roughly 1,500 appointees remain unreleased.

articles.title: I Investigated the Online Sports Betting Industry. DraftKings Shut Down My Account.

paras.t: Late last month, I was getting dinner on the table when an email hit my inbox with some bad news.
“Upon review your account has been closed at DraftKings’ discretion,” the message read. “We understand that this is not the decision that you were hoping for but this decision is final.”
I hadn’t bet on sports in months and had withdrawn all but a few cents of my balance. Why, I wondered, would my account even be under review? Was it something I’d said?

In September, I’d published an investigation into how online sports betting companies like DraftKings court customers — and whether the internal guardrails they’ve put in place to stop their users from spiraling out of control are firm enough. For that piece, I’d intentionally bet like a problem gambler, recklessly escalating my betting behavior over 10 weeks. My wagering had been informed by a panel of professional sports bettors, recovering addicts and addiction specialists.
As I flagrantly waved the red flags, DraftKings made me a VIP and assigned me my very own personal host. My recklessness was being rewarded. It just took three weeks and about $6,000 of losses.

The company, like the rest of the industry, says it doesn’t want to profit off of addiction, and has invested heavily in a system of tools and in-app prompts designed to help bettors put conditions on their gambling and slow them down. But my experiment raised serious questions about the effectiveness of this system, what’s known as “responsible gaming.”

So on one hand, I could understand how a story like mine, which scrutinized a core business function, might rankle company executives. But on the other hand, DraftKings had been downplaying the significance of my story for weeks.

In an interview for the piece, the company’s chief responsible gaming officer, Lori Kalani, had told me that the system “worked the way it was supposed to” in my case by feeding me some 30 responsible gaming messages over the course of my 10-week betting spree. And on Oct. 22, about a month after publication, DraftKings CEO Jason Robins doubled down, telling a CNBC journalist that he had “personally looked” at my entire betting history and was “pretty proud of how we handled it.” (He also made false claims about my reporting, but I’ve already addressed that on X.)
So as I read the notice of my account closure, I wondered: What changed, exactly?

DraftKings didn’t respond when I asked. All I got was a check in the mail for 94 cents, the remainder of my balance. But what was clear was that my investigation was reaching more and more people — including state regulators and federal lawmakers. Since publication, it had gone viral. A 27-minute, behind-the-scenes documentary of our work that we posted on YouTube on Oct. 10 had been viewed more than 6 million times in just three weeks.

The video offered viewers who may not be familiar with ProPublica (or perhaps not inclined to read 4,000-word stories) a way to learn about the reporting in the venue where so much sports betting content lives. Most of our viewers were young men — the prime sports betting demographic. And boy did they engage, leaving 3,500 comments on YouTube and flooding my inbox with messages about the same features and VIP perks detailed in my story.

Regulators from across the country were citing my investigation when announcing that they were going to take a look for themselves at how DraftKings and its ilk incentivize users to keep betting. Federal and state officials were also demanding answers about how the company lures in its customers and keeps them in the action. In Ohio, regulators were even proposing a rule to restrict the apps’ marketing practices that spoke directly to one of the findings in my piece.
On the morning of Oct. 27, I sent DraftKings a series of questions for a story about that impact.

That evening is when the unsigned notice from DraftKings Support about my account closure appeared in my inbox. Two hours later, the company sent me a formal response to my questions, writing, in part, that “regular conversations and check-ins with regulators are normal course of business” and denying that the company improperly targets losing gamblers.
I may no longer be able to access my account, but I’m still reporting on DraftKings and the online gambling industry.

In fact, right now, we’re collecting wagering data from bettors to better understand how the major operators handle problem gambling. You can help by submitting your data here. If you’ve got a tip, you can also reach me directly at 917-512-0276 and jake.pearson@propublica.org.

articles.title: I Photographed Her Parents as They Were Sentenced for Her Twin’s Death. Years Later, I Photographed Her Life.

paras.t: About eight years ago, I was assigned to photograph the sentencing of Travis and Sarah Mitchell, a couple with deep roots in an insular faith-healing sect outside of Portland, Oregon.

The Mitchells, as members of the Followers of Christ, adhere to a doctrine that forbids medical care. Instead, followers rely on healing through faith. So when Sarah Mitchell gave birth prematurely to twins in 2017 — and both gasped for breath in their first hours — the couple didn’t rush them to an emergency room. Instead, they turned to prayer.

One twin, Ginnifer, lived for four hours, each one a struggle. The family eventually sought medical care for her surviving twin sister, Evelyn, but only after the county’s deputy medical examiner arrived at the location of the home birth and learned, though not right away, of Evelyn’s existence. Even then, he had to seek help from police, who arrived at the Oregon City home and told reluctant family members to take the struggling infant to the hospital or they’d do it themselves.

The Mitchells pleaded guilty to criminally negligent homicide in the death of their infant daughter, Ginnifer, and to criminal mistreatment for failing to seek medical care for her surviving twin, Evelyn. The couple’s lawyer told the judge that the Mitchells grieved the loss of Ginnifer and loved Evelyn. “Travis and Sarah are utterly sincere, decent and caring human beings,” he told the judge. (The Mitchells and their lawyer did not respond to ProPublica and The Oregonian’s recent requests to be interviewed.)

Today, my memory of the sentencing is more montage than detail. But I remember the crowded gallery, the couple in black-and-white-striped prison clothing, and their prison sentence of more than six years. Evelyn, who within days of her birth had been placed in the custody of Marshall and Jennifer Phillips, another couple in the Followers of Christ, wasn’t present. She remained in the couple’s permanent care.
The Mitchells went off to prison, and I went on with my life.

Such is the grinding rhythm of the daily news cycle. So often I see people on their worst day — and then never again. Stories don’t really end, of course, but my role as a photojournalist is limited. I’m an observer rather than a participant, seeing mostly slivers of the human experience that offer only a window into the whole. It’s rare that I get to see what happens next.

Never would I have dreamed that the surviving baby in this case, Evelyn, would be someone I’d later come to know and care about through my work. But that’s precisely what happened eight years after that courtroom scene played out, when I began documenting the lives of Evelyn and her parents, the Phillipses. (In a legal filing in an ongoing case relating to Evelyn’s custody, the Mitchells criticized the Phillipses for allowing her to participate in our coverage.) The resulting story, a collaboration between ProPublica and The Oregonian, is one of several recently published about faith healing and the Followers of Christ church. It intimately explores the Phillipses’ journey out of the sect and illustrates how changes in Oregon state law — in contrast to neighboring Idaho, where the Followers have a handful of churches — have led to a reduction in child deaths.

To spend time around 9-year-old Evelyn is to behold a luminous, magnetic force of nature. It’s impossible to imagine this same girl as a premature baby so small that the only items that fit her were doll clothes purchased from the supermarket toy aisle.

For months, as I documented Evelyn’s life — from her baptism to her home life to doctors’ appointments — my journalism colleagues worked on their own pieces of our project. Teresa Mahoney, video editor at The Oregonian, produced a video introduction to the story that included a sequence of footage recorded by body cameras worn by police officers who stood outside Evelyn’s grandparents’ house that night, at first nudging, then ordering, Evelyn’s family to get her to the hospital. Each time I viewed it, as I watched the officers politely letting time slip away, I’d need to regulate my own breathing as I imagined Evelyn on the other side of that door, struggling to breathe herself.

I hope that reporter Noelle Crombie’s words, Teresa’s video and my photographs allow readers to see not only the journey of the couple who are raising Evelyn as their own but also the surviving — indeed, thriving — twin I came to know. That Evelyn is alive at all is, depending on your worldview, a miracle.
My work is all about observing and capturing moments, about freezing time. Here, I was witnessing the unfolding of time. I got to see what happened next.

articles.title: An atlas of vanished places: how climate change is rewriting the books on our shelves

paras.t: On August 26, 2026, a huge mass of rock and ice broke away at an altitude of around 5,200 metres in the Himalayas. Within minutes, it became an avalanche of debris and water that hurtled down towards the Nepal-Tibet border, with such force that the seismic signals were initially mistaken for an earthquake.

The region’s glaciers are visibly retreating, and thawing permafrost may well have contributed to destabilising these Himalayan slopes. Above all, the Nepal landslide illustrates something that will only become increasingly familiar: places that appear stable can change almost without warning.
While events like the Nepal landslide have an immediate, devastating impact on the people who live in these environments, they also leave their mark in a less obvious sphere: literature.

Biologist Rachel Carson’s 1951 book The Sea Around Us reminded readers that the boundary between land and sea has never been stable. Throughout our planet’s very long history, the oceans have advanced and receded. What makes the current situation exceptional is the speed of this transformation, as well as human activity’s decisive contribution to it.
Rising sea levels are one of its most visible manifestations. Since 1993, the global average sea level has risen by around ten centimetres.

And when a landscape changes, it also changes the world depicted in books. One scene from Lore Segal’s 2013 Half the Kingdom, for instance, takes place on a Brooklyn beach that a reader in the not-too-distant future might find submerged.

Philip Hoare’s The Sea Inside, also from 2013, explores coastal areas from England to Sri Lanka that may soon be underwater. The sandbanks of the Java Sea, where Joseph Conrad set his 1912 novel Freya of the Seven Isles, may have already been swallowed by rising sea levels.
When the landscape changes, these works all stay the same. Instead it is we, as readers, who change.
Reading from the future

The field of comparative literature has long been exploring how works take on new meanings as they circulate across eras and cultures. Climate change adds an unexpected dimension to this problem: the future can also influence the history of a work.

In 1888, Theodor Storm published The Rider on the White Horse. The novella’s protagonist, Hauke Haien, studies geometry and applies his knowledge to the construction of new dykes on Germany’s North Sea coast, convinced that they will stand for centuries. A major flood tests both Haien’s engineering feat, and humanity’s confidence in our ability to master the sea.

Storm, of course, was writing before global warming, but today we – unlike the author and his original readers – know that the conditions that determine the behaviour of coastlines are changing. This allows us to read his story differently today. Not because we have discovered what Storm “really meant”, but because we are reading it from a different future.
An unexpected atlas

Something even stranger can happen with the settings of literary works. Texts that we used to see as realistic might start to seem fantastical to us because they describe landscapes that no longer exist. And some works of fantasy might go the other way.

In Edgar Allen Poe’s only novel, 1838’s The Narrative of Arthur Gordon Pym of Nantucket, the author imagined a temperate region in Antarctica. When the book was published, it was a fantastical vision, but how will someone a hundred years from now interpret it?
Part of our library could thus become, without changing a single word, an unwitting atlas of vanished places. This is what lies at the heart of my research on literature, oceans and climate change.

Books do not predict the future, nor can they replace climatology, glaciology or oceanography. They do something else: they preserve experiences of places, and connect timelines that no single human life can encompass. When the world changes, landscapes do not disappear from the page – they remain there, exactly as they were. What changes is the way we read them.
